notes:
I've gathered extensive material from Enduring Word, Gill's Exposition, Ellicott's Commentary, and the Pulpit Commentary. From search result excerpts I also have Spurgeon's "Mongrel Religion" sermon and Constable's Expository Notes. Let me now compile verse-by-verse notes, drawing from what the sources actually say.

---

## 2 Kings 17:21–41 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 21 — The Root of the Evil: Jeroboam's Great Sin

- **Gill**: The rending of Israel from the house of David took place under Rehoboam, "signified by the rending of a garment in twelve pieces, ten of which were given to Jeroboam." It "is here ascribed to the Lord, being according to his purpose and decree." The people "made Jeroboam … king of themselves, without consulting the Lord and his prophets; and which was resented by him, though it was his will." Jeroboam "drave Israel from following the Lord; forbidding them to go up to Jerusalem to worship." The Targum renders it "made them to err." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: "The verse assigns the *fons et origo mali*; it makes the secession of the Ten Tribes from the house of David the ultimate cause of their ruin." Notes a textual issue: the Hebrew as it stands means "Israel rent" (intransitive), and the Vulgate reads "scissus est" (was rent). "Drave" — Hebrew text means "put far away"; Hebrew margin "misled." "The argument obviously is this — separation from Judah led to the calf-worship, and that to idolatry pure and simple." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Jeroboam not only introduced the worship of the calves, but he 'drave Israel from following the Lord' — i.e. compelled the people to discontinue the practice of going up to worship at Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:13-16), and required them to take part in the calf-worship." The separation alone might not have been fatal, but Jeroboam's idolatrous policy was the taint from which all other evils flowed. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)**: This was state-sponsored idolatry. It "did not immediately ruin the kingdom," yet it was "the beginning of the end." [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

### v. 22 — Persistent Walk in Jeroboam's Sins

- **Gill**: "They observed his injunction, not to go to Jerusalem to worship, and they worshipped the calves he did: they departed not from them: in all succeeding reigns, until the time of their captivity." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: "Israel obstinately persisted in the sin of Jeroboam, in spite of all warning." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The nation "continued to 'walk' in them — followed Jeroboam's example in 'all his sins' — gave up the temple-worship altogether; accepted the ministrations of priests not of the seed of Aaron; brought their tithes to these idol-priests; sacrificed to the calves at Dan and Bethel (Amos 4:4); and put their trust in the 'similitude of a calf that eateth hay.'" [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

---

### v. 23 — Removal from God's Presence into Exile

- **Gill**: "Until the Lord removed Israel out of his sight … as he had said by all his servants the prophets; by Hosea, Amos, Micah, and others." The phrase "unto this day" refers to the time of writing the book; "nor have they returned unto our days, nearly 2,800 years later." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: The land was not entirely depopulated (cf. 2 Chron 30:1; 34:9), but "the distinctive character of the nation was lost; such Hebrews as remained in their old land became mixed with their heathen neighbours." On the "lost tribes," Robertson Smith is quoted: "The problem of the lost tribes … is a purely fanciful one … Scattered among strange nations, they accepted the service of strange gods (Deuteronomy 28:64), and, losing their distinctive religion, lost also their distinctive existence." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Precept Austin**: This fulfilled Moses' warning in Deut 30:17–18 and the prophecy of Ahijah in 1 Kgs 14:14–16. Tens of thousands were deported; Sargon II boasted of carrying away 27,290 people from Samaria. [URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-17-commentary]

- **Enduring Word**: Some righteous Israelites from the north had already migrated to Judah in Jeroboam's day to escape idolatry (2 Chron 11:13–16), so "the 'lost tribes' were never truly lost." [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

### v. 24 — Assyrian Resettlement Policy

- **Gill**: The king of Assyria was either Shalmaneser or his son Esarhaddon (cf. Ezra 4:2). He brought people from Babylon, Cuthah (a place in Erech in Babylonia), Ava (perhaps a colony of the Avim), Hamath (a Syrian city on the northern border of Canaan), and Sepharvaim (possibly the Sippara of Ptolemy). "They possessed Samaria as an inheritance; sowed it with corn, and planted vineyards there." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: Sargon (Sargîna) records in his annals settling conquered Babylonians in "the land of Hatti" (Syria) and Arab tribes "in the land of Beth-Omri" and "in the city of Samerina" (Samaria). Kuthah (Kutie in inscriptions) had a temple of Nergal; Sepharvaim (Sipar/Sippar) means "the two Sipars," divided between the sun god Samas and the goddess Anunitum. "Placed them" translates the very phrase Sargon uses (*usesib*). [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Constable** (via search): Sargon II (722–705 BC) was probably the king. These imported foreigners eventually intermarried with Jews who remained and "probably were the ancestors of the Samaritans of Jesus' day (cf. John 4:9)." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Having removed the bulk of the native inhabitants, the Assyrians did not allow the country to lie waste, but proceeded to replace the population which they had carried off by settlers from other localities." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

---

### v. 25 — Lions Sent as Judgment

- **Gill**: The settlers "feared not the Lord; did not serve him in any manner, but their idols only, which they brought with them; whereas it was usual with Heathens to serve the gods of the country … but even this those men did not do." Lions came into their cities out of "the thickets of Jordan and other places where they haunted" (cf. Jer 49:19). [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: Lions multiplied naturally in the interval between depopulation and re-peopling. The settlers understood the ravages "as a token of the wrath of the local deity on account of their neglect of his worship. The sacred writer endorses this interpretation … probably remembering Leviticus 26:22." The verb form "implies a state of things which lasted some time." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word**: This shows "there was not only something special about the kingdom of Israel, but also something special about the land of Israel. God demanded to be feared among the people of the land, even if they came from other nations." Zech 2:12 calls it the Holy Land. [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

- **Spurgeon** (quoted by Enduring Word): "Always be somewhat diffident of your own conversion if you can trace it only and solely to motives of terror." [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

- **Spurgeon, "Mongrel Religion" sermon**: "He did send lions among them, and it was these lions that converted them. Their teeth and fangs and fiery eyes and the thunders of their roars converted them." But such fear-based religion is inadequate. [URL: search excerpt — sermon at spurgeon.org]

---

### v. 26 — The Settlers' Plea: "We Don't Know the God of the Land"

- **Gill**: The settlers took "Jehovah the God of Israel to be a topical deity, limited peculiarly to the land of Israel, whereas he was the God of the whole earth; a like notion obtained among the Syrians, see 1 Kings 20:28." The word translated "manner" is *mishpat* (judgment) — meaning "the laws, statutes, ordinances, and judgments, according to which he was worshipped." They perceived "it was not a common case … but the hand of a superior Being." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: *Mishpat* here means "appointed worship" or "cultus." He notes an interesting parallel: "In the Koran the word *din*, 'judgment,' is used in a similar way, as equivalent to 'religion.'" [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word**: "These Assyrian officials seemed to know what the recently-conquered kingdom of Israel did not know — that they had to honour the God of Israel." Yet their faith was "founded in simple fear of the lions — leading to an inadequate relationship with God." [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

### v. 27 — The King's Command: Send a Priest

- **Gill**: The king commanded, "Carry thither one of the priests whom ye brought from thence." The Hebrew has the plural "let them go," suggesting more than one priest. The Jews say two were sent, named Dosthai (or Dosithaeus) and Zachariah. Josephus likewise says "the people desired that priests might be sent to them of the captives." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

---

### v. 28 — A Corrupt Priest Teaches at Bethel

- **Gill**: This priest "was, doubtless, one of the priests of the calves; for there were none else in the kingdom of Israel carried captive." He chose to dwell at Bethel "where probably he formerly dwelt, and officiated in the service of the calf there." An Arabic writer says his name was Uzziah; Epiphanius says Esdras, "but he wrongly makes him to be sent by Nebuchadnezzar, thirty years after the captivity of the Jews in Babylon." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: He dwelt in Bethel "because he was a priest of the calf-worship." "Fear the Lord" is to be understood "not in the modern ethical but in the ancient ceremonial sense." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word**: "The priesthood of the kingdom of Israel was corrupt, but the king of Assyria did not know and was not interested in the pure religion of Israel. Therefore this nameless, corrupt priest taught the new inhabitants of the land a corrupt religion." It had elements of true faith but was "corrupted by the centuries of state-sponsored idolatry." [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

### vv. 29–31 — Each Nation Made Its Own Gods

- **Ellicott** on the deities:
  - **Succoth-benoth**: The Hebrew spelling "has probably suffered in transmission." The Babylonian goddess Zirbânit or Zarpanitum ("seed-maker"), consort of Merodach, appears to be meant.
  - **Nergal**: The god represented by the colossal lions guarding Assyrian palace doorways. "A syllabary informs us that Nergal was the god of Kutha."
  - **Ashima**: "Nothing is known of this idol." Identification with the Phoenician Esmûn is rejected by Schrader.
  - **Nibhaz and Tartak**: Unknown, "but the forms have an Assyrio-Babylonian cast."
  - **Adrammelech**: Identified by Schrader with Adar-mâlik, "Adar is prince."
  - **Anammelech**: Anum-mâlik, "Anu is prince." Both Adar and Anu are well-known Assyrian gods.
  - [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The Sepharvites "burned their children in the fire" to Adrammelech and Anammelech — this was the abominable Molech-style child sacrifice. The rabbinical writers said Nergal was worshipped as a cock, Ashima as a goat, Nibhaz as a dog, Tartak as an ass, and Adrammelech and Anammelech as a mule and horse. But "not much confidence can be placed in these representations." Babylonian gods were ordinarily figured in human forms, with animal forms (bull, lion, winged and human-headed) used only in a few cases symbolically. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Gill**: Each nation "continued to make gods of its own, and put them in the shrines on the high places which the Samaritans had made." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-kings-17.html]

---

### v. 32 — Priests from Every Class for the High Places

- **Ellicott**: "Of the lowest of them" — rather, "of all orders, or promiscuously" (compare 1 Kgs 12:31, where Jeroboam made priests from among all the people). "This is another indication that it was Jeroboam's mode of worship which was now restored." The verb "do" (*sacra facere*) is used in the sense of performing sacrifices. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "They feared the Lord, and from every class they appointed for themselves priests." The syncretism is so striking the writer cannot but dwell on it, repeating himself in vv. 32, 33, and 41. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Constable** (via search): "As polytheists the Assyrians did not hesitate to worship Yahweh as well as their other gods … They had no priestly caste but appointed anyone as a priest." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-17.html]

---

### v. 33 — They Feared the LORD Yet Served Their Own Gods

- **Ellicott**: "Literally, *Jehovah were they fearing, and their own gods were they serving*." The verse recapitulates vv. 28–32. The phrase "after the manner of the nations" means "according to the customs of the cities from which Sargon had deported them." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "This syncretism, this mixed religion, is so surprising to the writer, and so abhorrent to his religious sentiments, that he cannot but dwell upon it, not shrinking from repeating himself … in order to arrest the reader's attention, and point out to him the folly and absurdity of such conduct. The practice was still going on in his own day." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word**: David Guzik calls this a "'mongrel faith' that Pastor David applies directly to modern religious half-heartedness." It is the classic pattern of syncretism — adding the true God to a pantheon of false gods rather than serving Him exclusively. [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

### v. 34 — "To This Day … None of Them Worship the LORD"

- **Pulpit Commentary**: This apparent contradiction with vv. 32, 33, 41 ("they feared the Lord") is resolved: "The new immigrants 'feared Jehovah' in a certain sense, i.e. externally. They admitted him into their pantheon, and had ritual observances in his honor. But they did not really fear him in their hearts. Had they done so, they would have inquired what were his laws, statutes, and ordinances, and would have set themselves to obey them. This they did not think of doing." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Ellicott**: "They fear not the Lord" means "They fear Him not in the sense of a right fear; they do not honour Him in the way He has prescribed in the Torah." The LXX omits both negatives in this verse. The writer also has in mind "the remnant of the Ten Tribes who amalgamated with the new settlers" (cf. 2 Kgs 23:19; 2 Chron 34:6, 9, 33; John 4:12). [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Spurgeon, "Mongrel Religion"**: "Sometimes a verbal contradiction most accurately states the truth. They feared the Lord only in a certain sense; but, inasmuch as they also served other gods, it came to this when summed up, that they did not fear God at all. The man who is religious and also immoral, to put it in short, is irreligious." [URL: search excerpt from spurgeon.org]

---

### vv. 35–39 — The Covenant Obligation Recited

- **Constable** (via search): These verses contain "several loose quotations of passages from the Mosaic Law: Exodus 6:6; 9:15; 14:15–30; 20:4–5; 20:23; Leviticus 19:32; Deuteronomy 4:23; 4:34; 5:6; 5:15; 5:32; 6:12–13; and 7:11; 7:25." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word**: The covenant language echoes the first commandment and the Exodus redemption: "The LORD, who brought you out of the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. You are to bow down to Him and offer sacrifices to Him." This is the foundational covenantal demand for exclusive worship. [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The writer grounds the obligation in two things: (a) the Exodus redemption, and (b) the written statutes, ordinances, laws, and commandments. The repeated command "Do not worship other gods" (vv. 35, 37, 38) forms the refrain, and the positive command is to "worship the LORD your God, and He will deliver you from the hands of all your enemies" (v. 39). [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

---

### v. 40 — They Would Not Listen

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "Howbeit they did not hearken — The mixed race, with their mixed religion, though professing to be worshippers of Jehovah, paid no attention to the warnings and threatenings of the Law (v. 34), which were to them a dead letter. But they did after their former manner; i.e. they continued to maintain the syncretism described in vv. 28–33." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Enduring Word**: "But they would not listen, and they persisted in their former customs." This is the summary verdict — despite the clear covenant obligations, the mixed population persisted in their syncretistic ways. [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

### v. 41 — "So These Nations … to This Day"

- **Ellicott**: "The concluding words of the verse 'so do they unto this day' may be, and most probably are, taken from a document of earlier date than the compilation of the books of Kings. These carry the history down to about B.C. 560. The time between that date and the earlier days, when the priest sent from Babylon began to teach them something about Jehovah, may be taken in round numbers at a century and a half." In that period, the source document was written, and "when its author wrote the Samaritans were still idolaters." But change came gradually: "Yet even imperfect teaching about Jehovah produced its effect … they would be brought to see that Jehovah was more than any mere local divinity." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The mixed worship continued to the time of the composition of Kings (as late as 561 BC or 580 BC, cf. 2 Kgs 25:27). "It did not, however, continue much longer. When the Samaritans wished to join the Jews in rebuilding the temple (about 537 B.C.), they showed that inclination to draw nearer to the Jewish cult which henceforth marked their religious progress. Long before the erection of a temple to Yahweh on Mount Gerizim (409 B.C.) they had laid aside all their idolatrous rites, and, admitting the binding authority of the Pentateuch, had taken upon them the observance of the entire Law." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Spurgeon, "Mongrel Religion"**: "'So do they unto this day,' said the writer of the Book of Kings … Were he alive now he might say concerning the spiritual descendants of these Samaritans, 'So do they unto this day.' This base union of fearing God and serving other gods is by no means obsolete. Alas, it is too common everywhere … From generation to generation there have been Mongrel Religionists, who have tried to please both God and the devil, and have been on both sides, or on either side, as their interest led them." [URL: search excerpt from spurgeon.org]

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The final verse is a sober summary. "So these nations worshiped the LORD but also served their idols, and to this day their children and grandchildren continue to do as their fathers did." The pattern of syncretism was transmitted across generations. [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

---

## Tradition-Specific Insights

### Baptist View (Spurgeon)

Spurgeon's sermon "Mongrel Religion" directly expounds 2 Kgs 17:24–41. He identifies the settlers' faith as mere fear-driven religion: "He did send lions among them, and it was these lions that converted them." He warns: "Always be somewhat diffident of your own conversion if you can trace it only and solely to motives of terror." He calls this "a base union of fearing God and serving other gods" and says it is "by no means obsolete" — "Mongrel Religionists … have tried to please both God and the devil." He further notes the paradox: "They feared the Lord only in a certain sense; but, inasmuch as they also served other gods, it came to this when summed up, that they did not fear God at all." [Spurgeon excerpts found via search results from spurgeon.org and enduringword.com]

### Pentecostal / Charismatic View (Enduring Word — David Guzik)

Guzik emphasizes the spiritual principle that "when we give our hearts to false gods or split our loyalty between God and the world, we become like the empty things we worship." He highlights the Hebrew word *hebel* (vanity/emptiness) from v. 15 and extends the application: God's judgment comes "not at the height of sin but after 200 years of idolatry." The priest sent back to Bethel was corrupt, and the resulting religion was a "mongrel faith." Guzik directly applies this to modern religious half-heartedness. He also argues the ten tribes were never truly "lost" because righteous Israelites migrated to Judah in Jeroboam's day (2 Chron 11:13–16), countering British-Israelite theories. [URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-17/]

### Reformed / Evangelical (Constable)

Constable highlights the historical chain: the imported foreigners "eventually intermarried with the Jews who remained in the land and probably were the ancestors of the Samaritans of Jesus' day (cf. John 4:9)." He emphasizes that "as polytheists the Assyrians did not hesitate to worship Yahweh as well as their other gods." The section vv. 34–41 forms a climax where the writer recites the covenant demands (loose quotations from the Mosaic Law) to show the gravity of the syncretistic compromise. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-17.html]

### Anglican View (Ellicott)

Ellicott supplies the richest textual and archaeological detail. His notes identify the Assyrian deities by their cuneiform counterparts (e.g., Adrammelech = Adar-mâlik, Anammelech = Anum-mâlik). He notes the LXX omissions in v. 34. His conclusion on the "lost tribes" is thorough: "The problem of the lost tribes, which has so much attraction for some speculators, is a purely fanciful one." He traces how the Samaritan religion evolved from polytheistic syncretism to eventual Pentateuch-only monotheism. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

### Wesleyan / Methodist (Pulpit Commentary Homiletics)

The Pulpit Commentary's homiletic section (search excerpt) describes the syncretists as having "tried the experiment of serving the God and the gods of … tried the impossible." The homiletic application draws a direct parallel to all who attempt to serve both God and the world. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html and biblehub.com homiletics excerpt]

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (Constable, Ellicott — historical-critical notes)

- **Sargon II's inscriptions**: Both Constable and Ellicott note that Sargon claimed credit for taking Samaria and deporting 27,280 people, settling conquered peoples from Babylon and Arabia in their place. The Hebrew verb "placed them" (*made them dwell*) is the same term Sargon uses (*usesib*). [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-17.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]

- **The Samaritans' religious evolution**: Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary both trace the trajectory from polytheistic syncretism (8th century BC) → recognition of the Pentateuch → monotheistic worship on Mount Gerizim (temple built 409 BC). The mixed worship described in this chapter was transitional. [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-17.html]

- **Text-critical note on v. 21**: Ellicott notes that the Hebrew as it stands for "He rent Israel" is grammatically problematic — it can only mean "Israel rent," suggesting the *niphal* (passive) should be restored: "Israel rent himself away." The Vulgate reads "scissus est." [URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-17.html]
